# Living review protocol — template

```
Template version: 0.2
Title:                <title>
Protocol version:     <X.Y>   (see S5.2)
Status:               <draft | active | paused | closed>
Last updated:         <YYYY-MM-DD>
```

## How to use this template

This document is the research plan for one living review: a continuously updated collection of
references, the evidence they contain, and a synthesis of that evidence, maintained to inform policy
decisions and/or research.

- **Items.** Each item has a stable ID (e.g. `S2.3`), a **Prompt** (what to write) and a **Complete
  when** list (what a reviewer checks). Write the response under **Response**. If an item does not apply,
  write `n/a` and give a one-line reason. Do not delete items or renumber them.
- **Core vocabulary.** Every review in this family describes evidence in terms of three kinds of
  *element*:
  - **Outcome**: a state or change that matters to someone, intended or not (e.g. lower firm emissions, lower cost of capital, higher compliance costs).
  - **Mechanism**: a process through which something does, or fails to, bring about an outcome (e.g. peer benchmarking once emissions are public).
  - **Factor**: an intervention, design feature, condition or context that shapes whether, how or how strongly a mechanism operates (e.g. mandatory vs voluntary disclosure, strength of enforcement, firm size).

  A policy is itself a factor. Each review defines these more precisely for its own scope (S1.3).
- **Decision log.** Any judgment the written rules do not settle is recorded in the decision log
  (S5.1). This applies to search, coding and synthesis alike. The log is how independent replications
  and later versions can see where the rules ran out. Ambiguities that recur are the main trigger for
  changing the protocol.
- **Changing this protocol.** Change the protocol only through the change log (S5.2), with one change
  per entry.
- **Self-contained.** A protocol does not depend on, or refer to, any other protocol. Other living
  reviews can be used only as references, found and screened through S2 like any other source.

---

## S1. Scope

### S1.1 Purpose and users
**Prompt.** What decisions or research questions will this review inform, and for whom? If known, state
when those decisions are made.
**Complete when:**
- at least one named decision or research question, and at least one intended user, are stated;
- it is clear what would make the review useful or not useful to that user.

**Response:**

### S1.2 Focus
**Prompt.** State the focus as one sentence of the form: *"Map the outcomes, mechanisms and factors
[related to / underlying] [focal element or policy space] in [context]."*
**Complete when:**
- the focus sentence is written;
- the focal element or policy space is named precisely enough to decide what is in scope.

**Response:**

### S1.3 Element space
**Prompt.** Define what counts as an outcome, a mechanism and a factor *in this review*:
- the level of detail at which elements are recorded;
- whether elements start from a seed list or emerge entirely from coding;
- which seed elements, if any, there are.

Seed elements go in the element registry (S3.2).
**Complete when:**
- a working definition and one example exist for each element type;
- the level of detail is stated;
- the seed list (or "none") is entered in the registry.

**Response:**

### S1.4 Boundaries
**Prompt.** What is out of scope, and why? Cover policies, jurisdictions, time period, kinds of actor
and kinds of evidence, as applicable.
**Complete when:**
- every exclusion has a one-line reason;
- anything a user might reasonably expect to be included but is excluded is listed explicitly.

**Response:**

### S1.5 Review questions
**Prompt.** List the specific questions the synthesis (S4) must answer. Give each an ID (`Q1`, `Q2`, …).
**Complete when:**
- each question can be answered from coded records;
- each question names the elements or element types it concerns.

**Response:**

---

## S2. Search: collecting and curating references

### S2.1 Sources
**Prompt.** Where will references come from (databases, repositories, institutional websites, reference
lists, expert suggestions, …), and why are these sources enough for the focus?
Existing reviews, evidence maps and living reviews on related topics are references like any other and
may be listed here as sources.
**Complete when:**
- every source is named;
- any kind of reference the review deliberately does not search for is stated.

**Response:**

### S2.2 Search procedure and log
**Prompt.** How is each source searched? Give queries or procedures exactly enough to re-run, and say
what is logged for each search.
**Complete when:**
- each source has a re-runnable query or procedure;
- the log fields include at least: date, source, query or procedure, number of results.

**Response:**

### S2.3 Inclusion rules
**Prompt.** List the rules a reference must satisfy to be included. For each rule, give one example that
passes and one that fails.
**Complete when:**
- every rule has both examples;
- the rules together let someone without context decide most cases;
- borderline cases are routed to the decision log.

**Response:**

### S2.4 Screening procedure
**Prompt.** Specify:
- who or what applies the inclusion rules, at which stages (e.g. title/abstract, then full text);
- how many independent passes are made, and over what share of references;
- how disagreements are resolved;
- what is recorded for each reference.

**Complete when:**
- each reference's decision and reason are recorded;
- the checking method for screening consistency is stated (e.g. a share screened twice, agreement reported).

**Response:**

### S2.5 Updating
**Prompt.** When is the search re-run (schedule and/or triggers such as new policies or publications)?
How are new references handled, and how are earlier inclusion decisions preserved?
**Complete when:**
- the schedule or triggers are stated;
- earlier decisions are never overwritten, only superseded with a reason.

**Response:**

---

## S3. Coding and appraisal

### S3.1 Unit of coding
**Prompt.** What does one coded record represent (e.g. one claim or finding about a relationship between
elements, anchored to one passage)? How are these handled:
- references that report several findings;
- one finding reported in several references;
- findings that are reported second-hand (cited from another reference);
- summary claims in reviews or syntheses that aggregate other findings (e.g. "studies find reductions of 8–15%");
- findings where an element role is missing (e.g. a factor–outcome relationship with no mechanism stated)?

**Complete when:**
- the unit is defined;
- each of the five situations has a rule.

**Response:**

### S3.2 Element registry
**Prompt.** How are outcome, mechanism and factor elements created, named, defined, merged, split and
retired? The registry is a table with at least these columns:
- `ID` (`O-nn`, `M-nn`, `F-nn`, never reused);
- `name`;
- `definition`;
- `example record`;
- `broader element` (an element ID, to express hierarchy);
- `status` (active / merged into … / split into … / retired);
- `added_in` (the protocol version in which the element was added, e.g. `v0.2`).

**Complete when:**
- the procedure for adding, merging and splitting elements is stated, including who decides;
- the registry exists, even if it is empty apart from seeds.

**Response:**

### S3.3 Coding schema
**Prompt.** List the fields of a coded record. The core fields below are required; add any review-specific
fields with a definition and allowed values.

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `record_id` | unique, never reused |
| `reference_id` | the included reference |
| `passage` | short verbatim excerpt + locator (page/section) |
| `elements` | element IDs involved, each with its role in this record: outcome / mechanism / factor |
| `relationship` | one-sentence plain-language statement of what the passage claims about how the elements relate (including "no effect" or "effect only when …") |
| `context` | where/when/for whom the claim holds, as stated in the reference |
| `evidence_type` | from the list in S3.4 |
| `appraisal` | per S3.4 |
| `protocol_version` | version in force when coded |
| `coded_by` / `checked_by` | |

**Complete when:**
- every added field has a definition and its allowed values;
- one fully coded example record is included.

**Response:**

### S3.4 Appraisal
**Prompt.** Define:
- the evidence types used (e.g. causal estimate, association, description, theory, expert or stakeholder expectation, statement that evidence is lacking);
- what is judged about each record. At minimum: *strength* (how well the evidence supports the claimed relationship) and *relevance* (how directly it applies to this review's context). Add review-specific dimensions where the focus needs them (e.g. whether an outcome measure can separate real change from reporting artefacts);
- the scale and the rule for each level of each dimension.

**Complete when:**
- each level of each scale has a rule and an example;
- strength, relevance and any added dimension are recorded separately, not combined into one score.

**Response:**

### S3.5 Coding procedure and consistency
**Prompt.** Specify:
- who or what codes, and in how many passes;
- what share of records is coded independently twice, and how agreement is measured;
- how disagreements are resolved;
- what counts as a coding ambiguity that goes to the decision log.

**Complete when:**
- the procedure is stated;
- the share coded twice is stated;
- the agreement measure is stated.

**Response:**

### S3.6 Worked examples
**Prompt.** Provide worked examples that cover:
- each element role;
- each evidence type;
- at least one hard case (e.g. a "no effect" finding, a second-hand report, a passage involving several elements).

**Complete when:**
- every role and evidence type has at least one example;
- at least one hard case is included.

**Response:**

---

## S4. Synthesis

### S4.1 Outputs
**Prompt.** What does the synthesis produce, and in what form? Examples:
- an element map (which outcomes, mechanisms and factors are linked, and by how many records);
- a summary for each review question;
- a list of gaps.

**Complete when:**
- each output is named, with its format;
- each output is linked to the review questions (Q-IDs) it answers.

**Response:**

### S4.2 From records to statements
**Prompt.** How are coded records combined into synthesis statements? Cover:
- grouping, e.g. by outcome, then mechanism, then factor;
- the treatment of agreeing, conflicting and context-dependent records;
- what every statement must cite.

**Complete when:**
- the grouping rule is stated;
- the rule for conflicting records is stated;
- every statement must list the record IDs it rests on.

**Response:**

### S4.3 Confidence
**Prompt.** How is confidence in each synthesis statement judged from the appraisals of its records
(e.g. number, strength and consistency of records, relevance to context)? Give the levels and the rule
for each.
**Complete when:**
- each level has a rule;
- statements resting only on expectation or theory are labelled as such.

**Response:**

### S4.4 Gaps
**Prompt.** How are gaps identified and described? Examples:
- elements or links in scope with no records, or only weak ones;
- contexts in scope with no evidence;
- review questions that cannot be answered.

Say how gaps are prioritised against the purpose (S1.1).
**Complete when:**
- the gap types are defined;
- the prioritisation rule is stated.

**Response:**

### S4.5 Interpretation and limits
**Prompt.** How are findings related back to the decisions or research questions in S1.1? Address:
- which kinds of statement are not made (e.g. policy recommendations);
- how the limitations of the search, coding and synthesis are reported.

**Complete when:**
- the limits on what may be claimed are stated;
- a standing list of known limitations is kept.

**Response:**

### S4.6 Versions of the synthesis
**Prompt.** When is a new version of the synthesis issued? How are changes between versions reported
(statements added, revised or retired, each with the records or protocol changes that caused it)?
**Complete when:**
- the release trigger is stated;
- every change between versions can be traced to new records, recoding or a protocol change.

**Response:**

---

## S5. Maintenance

### S5.1 Decision log
**Prompt.** Where the log is kept, and its fields. Minimum fields:
- date;
- item ID (e.g. S2.3);
- case (reference or record ID);
- decision;
- reason;
- decided by.

**Complete when:**
- the log exists;
- it is reviewed at least once per synthesis version for recurring ambiguities.

**Response:**

### S5.2 Change log
**Prompt.** Record every change to this protocol as its own entry. Use this table:

| Change ID | Date | Item ID | Change (before → after) | Reason (link to decision-log entries or other evidence) | Effect on existing records (recode / flag / none) | Version after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Versioning:
- increment **X** when a change makes records or statements from earlier versions not directly comparable (e.g. scope, inclusion rules, element definitions, appraisal scales);
- increment **Y** for all other changes.

**Complete when:**
- each entry changes exactly one item;
- each entry gives a reason and states its effect on existing records.

**Response:**

---

| Version | Change |
|---|---|

review.title: What makes climate-related disclosure requirements effective? A living map of outcomes, mechanisms and factors
review.focus: Map the outcomes, mechanisms and factors related to the effectiveness of mandatory climate-related corporate disclosure requirements, across jurisdictions.

questions.text: Which outcomes are intended by in-scope requirements, and by whom? (outcomes)
For each intended outcome, which mechanisms are proposed and which are evidenced? (outcomes x mechanisms)
Which factors are reported to strengthen, weaken or block each mechanism? (mechanisms x factors)
Which unintended outcomes are reported or expected, through which mechanisms, and under which factors? (all)
Where is evidence absent, weak or confined to a few contexts? Prioritise by relevance to the S1.1 decision. (all)

registry.name: Market liquidity
registry.definition: Lower trading frictions from reduced information asymmetry among investors

registry.name: Firm cost of capital
registry.definition: Required return on a firm's equity or debt
registry.intended_by: UK FCA Listing Rule (P-107): cost of capital to 'better reflect' climate-risk management (REF-109 para 1.18); ISSB (P-06) Effects Analysis: lower cost of raising capital (REF-105 p.34)

registry.name: Firm GHG emissions
registry.definition: Emissions of firms subject to requirements
registry.intended_by: UK Government (Defra) for mandatory quoted-company GHG reporting (P-01): board attention as 'a driver for emissions reduction activity' (REF-108). Explicitly not intended by US SEC rules (P-105), which are 'agnostic' on climate-risk management (REF-107)

registry.name: Reporting quality & comparability
registry.definition: Informativeness and cross-firm comparability of what is reported
registry.intended_by: IFRS Foundation: 'decision usefulness of information' (REF-0001 p.14; REC-014 mission record). EU Directive 2014/95/EU: aims to 'harmonise non-financial disclosures' (as reported in REF-0018 s2 p.6, citing Zangheri & Farneti 2018; second-hand on the Directive); IFRS Foundation mission: decision usefulness (REF-0001 p.14; REC-014); EU NFRD (P-03) recital 3: comparability for investors and other stakeholders (REF-103, primary; replaces second-hand REF-0018 citation); EU CSRD proposal (P-102): adequate publicly available information (REF-101); UK Defra (P-01): 'true picture' of emissions (REF-117); ISSB IFRS S2 (P-06) BC1 (REF-104); IOSCO (REF-111); US SEC (P-105) (REF-107)

registry.name: Compliance cost
registry.definition: Direct cost of measuring and reporting
registry.intended_by: Reduction intended: EU CSRD proposal (P-102) specific objective to 'reduce unnecessary administrative costs' (REF-101; REF-102); ISSB (P-06) building on existing frameworks to reduce implementation costs (REF-105 p.9)

registry.name: Innovation / investment
registry.definition: Firms' investment and innovation activity

registry.name: Green capital reallocation
registry.definition: Shift of capital toward lower-carbon firms or projects
registry.intended_by: EU CSRD proposal (P-102): more financial resources to companies addressing social/environmental problems (REF-101; REF-102); UK FCA (P-107): 'drive investment towards greener projects' (REF-109 para 1.7)

registry.name: Information-asymmetry reduction
registry.definition: Public information narrows information gaps between investors

registry.name: Comparability spillovers
registry.definition: Standardised information lowers the cost of processing information about *other* firms

registry.name: Outside monitoring
registry.definition: Investors and analysts discipline managerial decisions

registry.name: Peer benchmarking
registry.definition: Firms learn their relative performance from peers' disclosures

registry.name: Internal measurement
registry.definition: Being required to measure creates information inside the firm itself

registry.name: Proprietary-cost exposure
registry.definition: Disclosure reveals commercially sensitive information to competitors

registry.name: Avoidance / boilerplate
registry.definition: Firms for which costs exceed benefits comply in form only

registry.name: Investor engagement & divestment
registry.definition: Responsible investors engage with firms or exit them

registry.name: Mandatory vs voluntary regime
registry.definition: Whether disclosure is required

registry.name: Enforcement & assurance
registry.definition: Supervision, sanctions and external assurance of reports

registry.name: Firm reporting incentives
registry.definition: A firm's own costs and benefits of informative reporting

registry.name: Firm size
registry.definition: Scale; determines fixed-cost burden

registry.name: Sector carbon intensity
registry.definition: Emissions intensity of the firm's sector

registry.name: Materiality basis
registry.definition: Financial vs double materiality

registry.name: Standard discretion
registry.definition: Choices left to firms (e.g. GHG Protocol boundaries, Scope 3 estimation)

registry.name: Institutional quality
registry.definition: Legal system, regulatory capacity; developed vs developing economy

registry.name: Non-GHG environmental & social performance
registry.definition: Firms' environmental (other than GHG) and social activities or performance, including pollutant releases, resource use and CSR/ESG activity measures. Direction coded as effect on performance (pollution reduction = +).

registry.name: Firm profitability / operating performance
registry.definition: Accounting profitability, margins or operating costs of firms subject to requirements

registry.name: Firm market value
registry.definition: Equity valuation (Tobin's q, P/E) or announcement returns to requirement events

registry.name: Anticipated regulation / future-cost pressure
registry.definition: Disclosure makes firms expect future regulation or future costs of their disclosed performance, prompting change

registry.name: Pre-mandate disclosure & performance
registry.definition: A firm's disclosure, information environment and performance on the disclosed dimension before the mandate (e.g. prior voluntary disclosure, prior ESG performance, emission level)

registry.name: Mandate implementation design
registry.definition: Who issues the requirement (government vs exchange/other) and its form (strict vs comply-or-explain)

registry.name: Stakeholder pressure / legitimacy threat
registry.definition: Public availability of a firm's disclosed performance exposes it to scrutiny by the public, NGOs, media or customers (not specifically investors), threatening its legitimacy and prompting change ('pillory effect')

registry.name: Informed decisions by investors and other users
registry.definition: Ability of investors, lenders, insurers and other report users to make informed decisions (investing, lending, underwriting, voting) using disclosed climate/sustainability information
registry.intended_by: TCFD (P-104; REF-106); UK Defra (P-01; REF-108); ISSB IFRS S2 BC17 and Effects Analysis (P-06; REF-104, REF-105); IOSCO (REF-111, REF-122); US SEC (P-105; REF-107); EU Commission on CSRD: investors' need for impact information (P-102; REF-102)

registry.name: Investor and consumer protection
registry.definition: Protection of investors (and, via financial firms, consumers) as a regulatory objective
registry.intended_by: US SEC (P-105): objective 'limited to' investor protection (REF-107); UK FCA (P-107): consumer protection (REF-109 para 1.12)

registry.name: Market pricing of climate-related risk and allocative efficiency
registry.definition: Asset prices, valuations and capital allocation across firms reflect climate-related risks and opportunities (market efficiency/integrity); distinct from O-07, which is a directional shift toward lower-carbon activity
registry.intended_by: TCFD (P-104; REF-106); UK FCA (P-107; REF-109); ISSB Effects Analysis (P-06; REF-105); IOSCO (REF-111); US SEC: market efficiency (P-105; REF-107)

registry.name: Financial stability / reduced systemic risk
registry.definition: Stability of the financial system and reduction of economy-wide systemic risk from mispriced climate or sustainability risk
registry.intended_by: FSB/TCFD (P-104; REF-106); EU CSRD proposal (P-102; REF-101); ISSB Effects Analysis (P-06; REF-105)

registry.name: Corporate accountability to society and stakeholders
registry.definition: Companies are held to account by the public, civil society and other stakeholders for their impacts on society and the environment
registry.intended_by: EU CSRD proposal (P-102; REF-101; REF-102); UN HLEG (P-108; REF-110)

registry.name: Economy-wide transition to a low-carbon / sustainable economy
registry.definition: Contribution of disclosure requirements to the transition of the economy and financial system toward net zero or sustainability
registry.intended_by: TCFD (P-104; REF-106); EU CSRD proposal (P-102; REF-101); UK FCA (P-107; REF-109). Explicitly not intended by US SEC (P-105; REF-107)

registry.name: Trust in and credibility of corporate sustainability information and commitments
registry.definition: Investors', consumers' and the public's trust in reported sustainability information and in corporate climate commitments (incl. net-zero pledges)
registry.intended_by: EU NFRD (P-03; REF-103); UN HLEG (P-108; REF-110)

registry.name: Harmonisation of requirements across markets
registry.definition: Consistency of reporting requirements across jurisdictions or Member States (single market, global baseline), reducing fragmentation
registry.intended_by: EU CSRD proposal: Single Market (P-102; REF-101); ISSB: comprehensive global baseline (P-06; REF-104)

registry.name: Investor climate-risk pricing
registry.definition: Investors use disclosed climate-related information to price risk, shifting valuations, cost of capital and capital flows across firms

registry.name: Public and stakeholder scrutiny
registry.definition: Civil society, consumers and the public use disclosed information to scrutinise firms and hold them to account (distinct from M-03, which covers investors and analysts)

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-04 (peer benchmarking). TESTED: under the US GHGRP, facility emissions fell 7.9% after disclosure, and channel tests support benchmarking: larger cuts by facilities revealed as more carbon-intense than peers, only once peer data were public, and falling within-industry dispersion (REC-015). PROPOSED only: for UK listed firms after the 2013 mandate, cross-firm comparison is offered as a consistent explanation of lower emissions, with no channel test verified (REC-021).
statements.confidence_reason: The mechanism is tested in one provisional CE record (abstract-level coding; full text re-checked only through a summarising fetch tool). The UK record counts for the emissions link only, not for the mechanism (S3.3 amended).
statements.conditions: Tested only for US facility-level reporting (P-02, data 2010-2013). UK firm-level (P-01) support is proposed only. Developed economies only.

history.blurb: First evidence: GHGRP facilities cut emissions after disclosure, with channel tests pointing to peer benchmarking.
Adds the UK 2013 mandate as a second setting where cross-firm comparison is offered as an explanation, but without a verified test, so the extension is to proposed status only.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-09 (anticipated regulation / future-cost pressure). TESTED: GHGRP facilities whose senators had more climate-progressive voting records cut emissions more after disclosure (cross-sectional, non-random variation) (REC-016). PROPOSED only: UK evidence is described as consistent with the mandate raising the expected future costs of high emissions (REC-021).
statements.confidence_reason: One provisional CE record tests the channel using cross-sectional variation the author describes as non-random; the UK record is proposed only.
statements.conditions: US 2010-2013 (tested) and UK after 2013 (proposed): periods when climate legislation was expected.

history.blurb: Introduces legislative concern as a tested driver of post-disclosure cuts in US facilities.
Adds a UK setting where future-cost pressure is proposed, without a verified test.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-05 (internal measurement). TESTED (null): in the one study testing it, two years of required measurement and private reporting to the regulator, before public release, produced no significant emissions response (REC-017). No record proposes M-05 for emissions.
statements.confidence_reason: Single provisional CE record (abstract coding; full text re-checked through a summarising tool).
statements.conditions: US GHGRP facilities, 2010-2011 private-measurement period vs 2012 onward.

history.blurb: Sole record: measurement without disclosure did not reduce emissions, so the channel is tested and not supported.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 with no tested mechanism: UK listed firms reduced absolute emissions after the 2013 mandate (about 8% in one published study, about 16% in another). US firms owning GHGRP facilities improved carbon intensity, measured with vendor (Trucost) data, but not absolute Scope 1 emissions. The size of the effect, and whether there is one, depend on the emissions measure and the level of analysis. Lower emissions among voluntary disclosers (AS) most likely reflect selection. The only mechanism these records offer is stakeholder pressure/legitimacy (M-10), and it is proposed only (see ST-18).
statements.confidence_reason: All CE records provisional; the AS record is Low and Indirect. The mechanism is not evidenced.
statements.conditions: Conditional on emissions measure (absolute vs intensity; reported vs vendor-estimated) and level (facility vs firm). Developed economies only (P-01 GB; P-02 US). REF-0001's summary range of 8-15% (p.12, not coded per S3.1) is below the 16% in the latest Jouvenot & Krueger abstract.

history.blurb: First public version (2019 working paper) shows UK-mandated firms cutting emissions relative to European controls; the published magnitude is about 8%.
A second UK study, also first public in 2019, finds a reduction, of about 16% in its 2021 revision.
US firm-level vendor data show gains in intensity only, so the effect depends on the emissions measure and level of analysis.
Voluntary disclosers' lower emissions are attributed to selection, cautioning against reading voluntary-disclosure associations as mandate effects.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-01 x M-01 (information asymmetry). TESTED: ESG disclosure mandates in 25 countries raised stock liquidity, and analysts' forecasts became more accurate and less dispersed, which bears directly on the information channel (REC-025). PROPOSED only: in the IFRS analogue, adoption alone had little liquidity effect, and the gains seen are tied to concurrent enforcement changes, with information asymmetry assumed rather than tested (REC-029, REC-030). After the UK carbon mandate, lower volatility and turnover are read as reduced uncertainty; the implication for liquidity is unclear (REC-012). The ESG and IFRS findings differ by instrument, so they are treated as conditional, not inconsistent.
statements.confidence_reason: All records provisional; IFRS records Indirect. M-01 is tested in one record, and that test is known from the authors' summary, not the full text.
statements.conditions: Liquidity gains appear where mandates are government-issued and enforced (ST-10, ST-11). ESG mandates 2000-2017 (multi-country); IFRS from 2005 (P-05).

history.blurb: IFRS analogue: mandatory adoption alone had little effect on liquidity.
Liquidity gains appear only with concurrent enforcement changes, with information asymmetry assumed rather than tested.
UK carbon mandate: lower volatility and turnover, read as reduced uncertainty (proposed), with unclear implications for liquidity.
ESG mandates across countries raise liquidity, and analyst-forecast evidence is the first record that tests the information channel.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-02 (cost of capital), no mechanism tested or proposed in the records: in the IFRS analogue, cost of capital fell and valuations rose only once anticipation before adoption is allowed for (REC-031). After the UK 2013 carbon mandate, newly disclosing firms' cost of equity fell (REC-022), except for the highest emitters, whose cost of equity rose (REC-023).
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional CE records only (author summary and abstracts).
statements.conditions: Direction depends on what disclosure reveals (F-09: emission level). UK P-01; IFRS P-05 (26 countries, 2001-2005).

history.blurb: IFRS analogue: lower cost of capital around mandatory adoption, conditional on allowing for anticipation.
Carries the finding to a climate mandate: UK newly disclosing firms' cost of equity fell.
The sign reverses for the highest emitters, so the effect depends on what is disclosed.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: M-02 (comparability spillovers), theory only. PROPOSED: standardisation creates externalities that firms do not internalise, so mandatory rules are needed for adequate comparability (REC-006). No record tests M-02 (see G-11).
statements.confidence_reason: Single TH record (second-hand).

history.blurb: Theoretical basis for a comparability externality that justifies mandates.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: M-02 (spillovers): effects on other firms are reported, but the channel is PROPOSED only. EU financial-statement disclosure regulation is reported to give positive information spillovers to other firms, especially larger ones (REC-035). The UK carbon mandate is reported to have had spillover effects on non-UK firms, with the outcome and sign unclear in the text read (REC-024). Neither record tests the comparability channel, and an ABS record says market-wide and externality effects are the least-studied part (REC-007).
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional CE records, one with unclear direction and one Indirect. The mechanism is not evidenced (all proposed).
statements.conditions: Analogue (P-08) and UK mandate (P-01) only.

history.blurb: Starts from a statement that market-wide and externality effects of disclosure regulation are scarcely evidenced.
First empirical report of positive information spillovers to other firms (financial-reporting analogue), channel not tested.
Reports cross-border spillovers of a climate mandate, but with unclear outcome and sign.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-02 (enforcement & assurance) strengthens effects. IFRS capital-market benefits arise only where legal enforcement is strong (REC-032), and liquidity effects only with concurrent enforcement changes (REC-030). Sustainability-reporting mandates have larger effects where law enforcement is stronger and assurance more widespread (REC-041). REF-0001 expects assurance and enforcement to be critical for CSR standards (EX, not counted). The mechanism linking enforcement to these outcomes is not tested in any of these records (M-01 is proposed in REC-030).
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional; two of three records Indirect (IFRS analogue).
statements.conditions: Analogue evidence dominates. Effect of enforcement on climate-specific outcomes (O-03) not studied in coded records.

history.blurb: IFRS analogue: capital-market benefits confined to strong-enforcement countries with transparency incentives.
Carries the enforcement/assurance moderation to sustainability-reporting mandates (country level).
Liquidity benefits appear only where enforcement changed concurrently, separating enforcement from the standards themselves.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-10 (implementation design): liquidity gains from ESG mandates are strongest when the requirement is issued by government institutions (with strong informal enforcement). In the same study the information channel (M-01) is tested through analyst forecasts.
statements.confidence_reason: Single provisional CE record.
statements.conditions: Multi-country ESG mandates, 2000-2017.

history.blurb: Sole record: government-issued mandates show the largest liquidity gains.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-09/F-03 (pre-mandate position and reporting incentives) shape responses. Effects are concentrated in, or reverse for, firms whose prior disclosure or performance was weak: highest emitters face a higher cost of equity, weak prior ESG performers have negative market reactions, and NFRD real effects are concentrated in firms with low prior CSR. IFRS benefits require firm incentives for transparency. None of these records states a mechanism.
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional.
statements.conditions: Different outcomes per record (O-02, O-10, O-08, O-01); agreement is on the direction of moderation, not on one outcome.

history.blurb: IFRS analogue: benefits depend on firms' incentives for transparency.
EU NFRD: negative market reaction concentrated in firms with weak pre-regulation ESG performance.
UK carbon mandate: cost of equity rises for the highest emitters.
EU NFRD real effects concentrated in firms with low prior CSR reporting and activity.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-04 (size): in the financial-reporting analogue, mandated disclosure deters innovation mostly among smaller firms, while larger firms benefit from information spillovers. Proprietary costs (M-06) and spillovers (M-02) are offered as the channels but are PROPOSED only in the text read. REF-0001 expects this to apply to granular CSR disclosures, less to aggregate GHG figures (EX).
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional and Indirect (analogue); channels not tested in the text read.
statements.conditions: Transfer to climate disclosure is an expectation (see ST-17), not evidenced. European data 2000-2018 (P-08).

history.blurb: Smaller firms' innovation is most deterred by mandated disclosure.
Larger firms gain from spillovers, so the size effect runs in opposite directions for small and large firms.

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: O-08 (non-GHG E&S performance): mandates are followed by improved E&S performance in four mandate countries (resource use), China (pollution) and the EU NFRD (CSR activities, Fiechter et al.). But a study excluding UK firms finds no NFRD improvement and attributes the positive EU result to UK firms. A UK study finds mandatory GHG disclosure reduced CSR engagement; REF-0001 attributes this to required measurement (M-05), proposed only. Context (UK inclusion) partly explains the NFRD conflict, but no coded context explains the negative UK CSR finding, so the statement is labelled inconsistent.
statements.confidence_reason: Conflicting provisional CE records. Per S4.2, the unexplained conflict (REF-0011 vs REF-0018's UK attribution) makes the statement inconsistent.
statements.conditions: Measures differ (pollutants, resource use, ESG ratings, CSR scores); ratings-based outcomes are a borderline case (S2.3). Policies: P-03, P-04, P-01; multi-country mandates without a policy entry.

history.blurb: Firm-level evidence of lower energy, waste and water use after sustainability-reporting mandates in four countries.
Adds China: lower industrial wastewater and SO2 in the cities most affected by the 2008 mandate.
UK GHG disclosure mandate associated with lower CSR ratings, against the positive direction.
EU NFRD: in-scope firms increased CSR activities.
Excluding UK firms, the NFRD shows no improvement in E&S scores.
Attributes the positive NFRD result to UK firms, explaining the NFRD conflict but leaving the REC-036 conflict unexplained.

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: Unintended outcomes reported (empirical): a negative average equity reaction to the EU NFRD, lower profitability after China's CSR mandate, fewer innovating firms under financial-statement mandates, lower CSR engagement in the UK, a higher cost of equity for the highest emitters, and more generic E&S disclosure after mandates. The channels offered for these, proprietary costs (M-06), avoidance/boilerplate (M-07) and required measurement (M-05), are all PROPOSED only. On profitability, a UK GHG-mandate study finds no change in gross margins, while the China study finds lower profitability; no coded context explains this, so the profitability evidence is inconsistent.
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional. The O-09 part is labelled inconsistent within the statement: instrument and jurisdiction differ, but no record shows that they explain the difference.
statements.conditions: Profitability: China CSR-report mandate (P-04) vs UK GHG mandate (P-01).

history.blurb: First reported cost: negative average equity reaction to EU NFRD legislative events.
Adds lower profitability after China's 2008 CSR mandate.
UK GHG mandate left gross margins unchanged, conflicting on profitability.
Adds fewer innovating firms under financial-statement mandates (analogue); proprietary-cost channel proposed.
Adds lower CSR engagement after the UK GHG mandate.
Adds a higher cost of equity for the highest-emitting new disclosers.
Adds more generic E&S disclosure after mandates; boilerplate channel proposed.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-04 x M-07 (avoidance/boilerplate). PROPOSED only: after E&S mandates, annual-report disclosure became more generic, while voluntary-framework adopters disclose less generically (REC-027, REC-028). Form-only compliance by poor-incentive firms is REF-0001's interpretation of this pattern; it is not tested in the text read.
statements.confidence_reason: AS records, provisional; voluntary comparison is Indirect and subject to selection. The mechanism is not evidenced.
statements.conditions: Global annual reports, 2001-2020.

history.blurb: Disclosure becomes more generic after mandates; boilerplate offered as the explanation.
Voluntary-framework adopters move the other way, which sharpens the contrast but is subject to selection.

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: Expected (not evidenced) effects in REF-0001: boilerplate avoidance by poor-incentive firms; wider real effects under double materiality; dependence on assurance and enforcement; divergent effects between developed and developing economies, possibly less convergence; proprietary costs for granular disclosures and smaller firms; investors' exclusionary screens as a cost to high emitters and a reallocation channel. All mechanisms named here are proposed.
statements.confidence_reason: EX records only; never merged with empirical statements (S4.3).

history.blurb: Expectation that poor-incentive firms will comply in form only.
Adds the expectation of wider real effects under double materiality.
Adds dependence on assurance and enforcement infrastructure.
Adds divergent effects across developed and developing economies.
Adds proprietary costs for granular disclosures, especially for smaller firms.
Adds investors' exclusionary screens as a cost and a reallocation channel.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-10 (stakeholder pressure / legitimacy threat). PROPOSED only: two studies of emissions after mandates explain their results by public exposure. For UK listed firms, a 'pillory effect' of stakeholder pressure is hypothesised (REC-018). For US GHGRP firms, a threat to legitimacy is put forward (REC-044). Neither study measures pressure or tests heterogeneity by visibility.
statements.confidence_reason: The mechanism rests only on explanations offered alongside CE results. Under amended S3.3 it does not count as evidenced, so it is graded like TH/EX (decision log). The factor-outcome link is graded in ST-05.
statements.conditions: UK (P-01) and US (P-02) only.

history.blurb: Introduces stakeholder pressure ('pillory effect') as the hypothesised channel for UK emission cuts.
A US firm-level study offers the same kind of explanation (legitimacy threat), again untested.

statements.question: Q1
statements.text: Reporting quality and comparability (O-04) is the most widely shared intended outcome: it is stated by the UK Government for GHG reporting (2012), the EU NFRD (2014) and CSRD proposal (2021), the ISSB (2023), IOSCO (2023) and the US SEC (2024), and by the IFRS Foundation's mission. The intended beneficiaries differ: investors only (SEC, ISSB, IOSCO) versus investors and other stakeholders (UK, EU).
statements.confidence_reason: Statement rests on INT records, which have no strength rating and are never evidence that the outcome occurs (S3.4); S4.3 gives no level for them (decision log; proposed change). Certainty concerns only that the named bodies state these aims, each read in the primary policy document. REC-014 is a pilot DE record that should be recoded INT under CH-004 (left to the data_v2 recoding).
statements.conditions: Who the information is for varies with materiality basis (F-06).

history.blurb: UK Government states that GHG reporting should give investors and stakeholders a true picture of company emissions.
EU NFRD adds comparability for investors and other stakeholders across the EU.
CSRD proposal restates adequate public information for users as a specific objective.

reviews.run_notes: Pilot run of protocol A v0.2 by a single agent. 26 references screened (18 included: seed + 11 seed citations + 3 backward + 3 web search; 8 excluded). 48 records (14 from REF-0001, 34 from primaries); 17 synthesis statements; 8 typed gaps. Nearly everything is provisional/Low by construction, because primaries were read only as abstracts, author summaries or tool-mediated full text. Main protocol problems: (1) Q2 'proposed vs evidenced' cannot be recorded (no mechanism-status field). Most empirical records state no mechanism, and S4.4 has no gap type for that. (2) intended_by is 'to code' for most outcomes, so gap type (a) and the Q1-first priority rule cannot yet be applied. (3) Outcome measurement (intensity vs absolute; vendor-estimated vs reported; ESG ratings) drives the main conflicts but has no appraisal dimension. (4) S1.4 and worked example REC-003 disagree on voluntary-only studies. (5) S4.3 has no rule for DE records. Substantive observations: REF-0001's 8-15% summary range sits below the latest Jouvenot & Krueger abstract (~16%). Downar et al.'s magnitude differs between working-paper (14-18%) and published (~8%) versions. de Villiers et al. (2024) attribute the positive NFRD result of Fiechter et al. (2022) to UK firms. Seed elements M-03 (outside monitoring) and F-05 (sector carbon intensity) have no records; S4.4 has no gap type for a mechanism with zero records. || Iteration 2 (protocol v0.9): recoded all 48 records with mechanism status (6 tested, 17 proposed mechanism mentions), policies (8 entries P-01..P-08), jurisdictions, period and evidence_year (38 verified from earliest public versions, 10 fallback). One new element (M-10 stakeholder pressure). Synthesis regenerated: Q2 statements separate tested and proposed mechanisms. One statement added (ST-18) and four type-(e) gaps (G-09..G-12); all non-Q1 statements and gaps carry a history. ST-01 (Q1) copied unchanged for replacement by the Q1 search. Main issues: only Tomar (M-04, M-05, M-09) and Krueger et al. (M-01) test a mechanism, so every other mechanism is proposed. Seven records lack sourced sample years. Ordering by evidence_year rests on fallbacks for 5 sources. | Q1 search: Targeted Q1 search (SL-101..SL-117) using web search and fetch. Screened 23 references (REF-101..REF-123): 13 included under I4, 8 excluded (date sources or duplicates), 2 unretrievable (COM(2021) 189; HLEG full report). Coded 45 records (REC-101..REC-145): 44 INT and 1 EX (a Defra IA claim of uncited evidence); 3 are same_as. Policies P-03..P-108, including the SEC rules' later status: stayed April 2024, defense ended 27 Mar 2025, and the 8th Circuit holding the case in abeyance (Apr and Sep 2025); no rescission sourced. intended_by filled for O-02, O-03, O-05 and O-07, and extended for O-04. Added O-50..O-57 and M-50..M-51. O-01, O-08 and O-10 remain 'to code'. Main finding: comparability (O-04) is the shared aim. Investor-focused instruments (TCFD, ISSB, IOSCO, SEC) add decision-usefulness, pricing and stability. The EU adds accountability, trust and an economy-wide transition (double materiality). The SEC explicitly disclaims climate or transition aims, and only the UK 2011 IA intends firm emission reductions. Caveat: passages come via WebFetch extraction (see deviations).

statements.conditions: US facility-level reporting (from 2010) and UK listed firms (from 2013); developed economies only.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-09 (anticipated regulation / future-cost pressure): emission reductions after mandated disclosure are attributed to firms' concerns about future legislation or future costs of high emissions.
statements.confidence_reason: Two provisional CE records (abstracts).
statements.conditions: US and UK, 2010s, a period of anticipated climate legislation.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03 x M-05 (internal measurement): in the one study testing it, required measurement without public disclosure did not appear to reduce emissions.
statements.confidence_reason: Single provisional CE record.
statements.conditions: US GHGRP facilities.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-03, mechanism unstated: mandated GHG disclosure is followed by lower absolute emissions for UK listed firms (about 8% in one study, about 16% in another). For US firms owning GHGRP facilities, firm-level vendor (Trucost) data show lower carbon intensity but no fall in absolute Scope 1 emissions. The size and even the presence of a reduction depend on the emissions measure and level of analysis. Lower emissions among voluntary disclosers (AS) are most likely selection.
statements.confidence_reason: All CE records provisional; the AS record is Low and Indirect.
statements.conditions: Conditional on emissions measure (absolute vs intensity; reported vs vendor-estimated) and level (facility vs firm). Developed economies only. REF-0001's summary range of 8-15% (p.12, not coded per S3.1) is below the 16% in the latest Jouvenot & Krueger abstract.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-01 x M-01 (information asymmetry): ESG disclosure mandates are associated with higher stock liquidity across countries. In the financial-reporting analogue, IFRS adoption alone had little liquidity effect, and the gains seen are tied to concurrent enforcement changes (see ST-10). The two sets differ in instrument, so the conflict is treated as conditional, not inconsistent. A reported fall in turnover after the UK carbon mandate has unclear implications for liquidity.
statements.confidence_reason: All records provisional; IFRS records are Indirect.
statements.conditions: Liquidity gains appear where mandates are government-issued and enforced (ST-10, ST-11).

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-02 (cost of capital), mechanism unstated: newly disclosing UK firms' cost of equity fell after the 2013 carbon mandate, except for the highest emitters, whose cost of equity rose. In the IFRS analogue, cost of capital fell and valuations rose only once anticipation effects before adoption are allowed for.
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional CE records only (author summary and abstracts).
statements.conditions: Direction depends on what disclosure reveals (F-09: emission level).

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: M-02 (comparability/information spillovers), theory: standardisation creates externalities that firms do not internalise, so mandatory rules are needed for comparability.
statements.confidence_reason: Single TH record (second-hand).

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: M-02 (spillovers), empirical: the UK carbon mandate is reported to have had spillover effects on non-UK firms (sign and outcome unclear in the text read). EU financial-reporting regulation gives positive information spillovers to other firms, especially larger ones. Market-wide and externality effects remain the least-studied part, per an ABS record.
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional CE records, one with unclear direction, one Indirect.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-02 (enforcement & assurance) strengthens effects. IFRS liquidity effects appear only with concurrent enforcement changes, and capital-market benefits only where enforcement is strong. Sustainability-reporting mandates have larger E&S effects where law enforcement is stronger and assurance more widespread. REF-0001 expects assurance and enforcement to be critical for CSR standards (EX, not counted).
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional; two of three records Indirect (IFRS analogue).
statements.conditions: Analogue evidence dominates. Effect of enforcement on climate-specific outcomes (O-03) not studied in coded records.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-10 (implementation design): liquidity gains from ESG mandates are strongest when the requirement is issued by government institutions (with strong informal enforcement).
statements.confidence_reason: Single provisional CE record.
statements.conditions: Multi-country ESG mandates.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-09/F-03 (pre-mandate position and reporting incentives) shape responses. Effects are concentrated in, or reverse for, firms whose prior disclosure or performance was weak: highest emitters face higher cost of equity, weak prior ESG performers have negative market reactions, and NFRD real effects are concentrated in firms with low prior CSR. IFRS benefits require firm incentives for transparency.
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional.
statements.conditions: Different outcomes per record (O-02, O-10, O-08, O-01); agreement is on the direction of moderation, not on one outcome.

statements.question: Q3
statements.text: F-04 (size): in the financial-reporting analogue, proprietary costs of mandated disclosure deter innovation mostly among smaller firms, while larger firms benefit from spillovers. REF-0001 expects this to apply to granular CSR disclosures, less to aggregate GHG figures (EX).
statements.confidence_reason: Provisional and Indirect (analogue).
statements.conditions: Transfer to climate disclosure is an expectation (see ST-17), not evidenced.

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: O-08 (non-GHG E&S performance): mandates are followed by improved E&S performance in China (pollution), four mandate countries (resource use) and the EU NFRD (CSR activities, Fiechter et al.). But a study excluding UK firms finds no NFRD improvement and attributes the positive EU result to UK firms. A UK study finds mandatory GHG disclosure reduced CSR engagement. The NFRD conflict is partly explained by context (UK inclusion), but the negative UK CSR finding is not explained by any coded context, so the statement is labelled inconsistent.
statements.confidence_reason: Conflicting provisional CE records; per S4.2 the unexplained conflict (REF-0011 vs REF-0018's UK attribution) makes the statement inconsistent.
statements.conditions: Measures differ (pollutants, resource use, ESG ratings, CSR scores); ratings-based outcomes are a borderline case (S2.3).

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: Unintended outcomes reported (empirical): fewer innovating firms under financial-statement mandates (M-06), lower profitability after China's CSR mandate, a negative average equity reaction to the EU NFRD, more generic E&S disclosure after mandates (M-07), higher cost of equity for the highest emitters, and lower CSR engagement in the UK. On profitability, a UK GHG-mandate study finds no change in gross margins, while the China study finds lower profitability; no coded context explains this, so the profitability evidence is inconsistent.
statements.confidence_reason: All provisional; O-09 part labelled inconsistent within the statement (instrument and jurisdiction differ, but no record shows they explain the difference).
statements.conditions: Profitability: China CSR-report mandate vs UK GHG mandate.

statements.question: Q2
statements.text: O-04 x M-07 (avoidance/boilerplate), empirical: after E&S mandates disclosure became more generic, while voluntary-framework adopters disclose less generically. This is consistent with poor-incentive firms complying in form only.
statements.confidence_reason: AS records, provisional; voluntary comparison is Indirect and subject to selection.
statements.conditions: Global annual reports.

statements.question: Q4
statements.text: Expected (not evidenced) effects in REF-0001: boilerplate avoidance by poor-incentive firms; divergent effects between developed and developing economies, possibly less convergence; wider real effects under double materiality; proprietary costs for granular disclosures and smaller firms; dependence on assurance and enforcement; investors' exclusionary screens as a cost to high emitters and a reallocation channel.
statements.confidence_reason: EX records only; never merged with empirical statements (S4.3).

gaps.text: O-04 (reporting quality & comparability, the only outcome with an established intended_by) has no records in developing economies; only an expectation (EX) that effects differ sharply there.
gaps.priority_reason: Intended outcome (Q1) and affects the many developing jurisdictions adopting ISSB-based standards.

gaps.text: ABS: the degree to which GHG Protocol discretion (boundaries, gases, classification) impedes comparability is under-researched.
gaps.priority_reason: Bears on intended outcome O-04; applies to every jurisdiction using IFRS S2/GHG Protocol.

gaps.text: ABS: costs of (sustainability) reporting requirements are largely unstudied; size-scaling of costs rests on expectation only, and no CE/AS record measures compliance cost.
gaps.priority_reason: Not an intended outcome, but central to the S1.1 decision (REF-0001 asks for criteria on pace and coverage by firm type); all jurisdictions.

gaps.text: ABS: market-wide effects and externalities of disclosure regulation, the main economic case for mandates, are scarcely evidenced. One provisional spillover record has unclear direction.
gaps.priority_reason: Underpins comparability (O-04, intended); all jurisdictions.

gaps.text: ABS (dated 2021): limited evidence on liquidity effects of CSR reporting. Partly addressed since by one multi-country study (REF-0006).
gaps.priority_reason: O-01 intended_by not yet established; multi-jurisdiction.

gaps.text: O-03 (GHG emissions) has no records outside the US and UK, none in developing economies, and none by firm size (F-04). Effects of enforcement (F-02) on emissions outcomes are unstudied in the coded set.
gaps.priority_reason: O-03 intended_by 'to code' (cannot be ranked as intended yet); affects every non-US/UK jurisdiction.

gaps.text: M-08 (investor engagement & divestment) has only an EX record. No coded study shows disclosure requirements operating through engagement or exclusion, and O-07 (green capital reallocation) has no empirical record.
gaps.priority_reason: O-07 intended_by 'to code'; relevant to all jurisdictions.

gaps.text: F-06 (materiality basis) and F-05 (sector carbon intensity) have no empirical records for any outcome; F-06 has one EX record.
gaps.priority_reason: Design choice live in ISSB vs ESRS jurisdictions, but no intended outcome directly affected in coded set.
